utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. Presentation is exactly as it was yesterday. Mr. Haynes, good morning to you, good morning, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to finish today? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm touch and go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Touch and go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Might do, might not do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I reckon if you stick to the 30 hours, you have about five hours left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Four and a half, five.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If I do just finish before the end of the day, I may crave your indulgence to allow me to think about it overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, we left off yesterday afternoon with the regular combat report of the 26th of September of 1995. I want to just step back a day and have a look at a few documents with you, and I want to start with P2925, please. This is translated but that shouldn't trouble anybody because it's simply a list of names. It's probably perfectly obvious to us all what this is, but since it isn't translated into English, can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a record of the presence of personnel in the command of the infantry brigade for September 1995. And on this list, we have all the officers and NCOs that were deployed in the command of the Zvornik Brigade so it's the records for the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if we just concentrate on entry number 31, that's you, is it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not highly ranked on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think that's because it's alphabetical but there you go. Can you help us, please, there appear to be three different entries in relation to your name. Firstly, we see what appears to be a T, what does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: T is terrain and probably there should be a legend at the end explaining what the Ts are. That means presence in the field or terrain and absent or free were the other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, the Ts appear to end on the 17th of September and then we see C. What does C stand for?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the Cyrillic S in actual fact which means that I was Slobodan, S as in Slobodan which means free, that I was not at work on duty that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that --

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a day off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that covers all the days from the 18th and including the 25th. On the 26th to the end of the month there appears to be a cross or a plus sign, what does that denote?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that I was at the command during those days and occupying my post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we now please have a look at 7D679, the regular combat report for the 25th of September. Thank you. Paragraph 2: "A team of officers from the brigade command is analysing operational tasks carried out last month while working on the operational tasks plan for the coming month. A training course is being prepared for platoon and squad commanders in the brigade. At 1500 hours, the brigade commander having returned from the corps where he presented his report, held a meeting with the battalion/artillery battalion commanders and core members of the command."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: To whom does that refer?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to Dragan Obrenovic. On that day, he was at the command in Vlasenica in the Drina Corps at a meeting linked to taking on assignments and the departure of the brigade to Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we go to the foot of this report which is page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This document appears to be type signed in your name, can you identify for us, please, the duty officer on the 25th of September who compiled this report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the initials MN, means that the person with those initials compiled this combat report and on the list of the command of the Zvornik Brigade, there is not a single person with these initials and they weren't on the list of duty operatives in the command of the Zvornik Brigade, either. However, he was in the rear, in the rear battalion, the logistics battalion. There was a man called Milutin Nedeljkovic who was a reserve captain who, from time to time, would be mobilised so most probably in September that was the case because of the lack of officers so he was probably on duty, and he didn't have a complete knowledge of the situation and the state of affairs and so quite logically he put my name as a signature believing that to be the proper way. I saw this report on the 17th of September, as well, a report of this kind with the same initials compiled by the same person, and he placed my name there but signed it Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Two more documents to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I see the previously document again, P2925, the records of presence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check where -- on what day the letter S begins and what day it ends. I was not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The first S appears on the 17th and the last S appears on the 25th. Would it help you if I handed you a hard copy and a hard-edged piece of paper so you could do the exercise I've just done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was mistaken. The first C appears on the 17th, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I may have said 18th, you might be correct, and I thank you very much for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We were just about to move very quickly to look at the duty operations officer's log book for P -- for the 25th of September, that's P379. If you can have the hard copy document again, you're going to look for page 547 and the rest of us at page 139.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you have the page we now have in e-court, General Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Since the date is not obvious on that page, can you just confirm that that page refers to the 25th of September?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This page should be the 26th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I want you to look down that page at two entries, please. One about a third of the way down, a meeting of battalion commanders at 1200 hours. Does that have any point of reference for you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should mean that a meeting was held of the battalion commanders at 1200 hours and perhaps the operative log book would provide better references for us to be able to be absolutely certain of what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: All right. But a few lines below that, we see: "Briefing at 10.00 as planned, Obren." What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here most probably there was some misunderstanding that Obrenovic had called a number of meetings not knowing that he was going to go to Krajina as command of the brigade, so this appears here twice, this referring at -- reporting at 1200 hours and the other at 1000 and the name Obren. So I'm not quite sure but at any rate, one of those two reporting sessions were held on that day, the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we may come back to that in another document but just one last document for your comments which bears the date the 25th of September, and it's P2927. And I'm going to be asked that you be provided the original of this document which I know is in court at the moment. Firstly, tell us, what is this document, what's the effect of it and what's its purpose?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is an order to form an infantry company which was supposed to become part of the Drina Brigade with the assignment in Zvornik and the 1st Krajina Corps. Now since the Zvornik Brigade provided one battalion, which was the special forces, the rear special forces, and this company, which was formed from men from the -- other battalions, this order came after the meeting which was held by Dragan Obrenovic which the commanders of the battalions and artillery battalions and regulated all these questions, and this order was later written according to the initials MN -- MM, Milan Maric, who was a clerk in the operative organ of the Zvornik Brigade staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If we go to the bottom of the document which is page 5 in the English and I think page 3 in the B/C/S but ... yes. It appears to bear a signature, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you sign that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a signature over a stamp, that's quite obvious, but usually you put the signature first and then the stamp because the order, or, rather, the person working in the offices of the headquarters should never place a stamp where there's no signature, and this shows that I signed this order on the 26th, that is to say, the following day, when I came to brigade headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think in fact, so that everybody can see that point, they better have a look at the original document that you have. Can you hand it first to Mr. McCloskey and then Their Honours may want to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's okay, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with the part about the stamp. When it was signed, I might have a disagreement with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. It can go back to Janet now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at brigade command on the 26th of September, what did you set about doing?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I met Obrenovic for a brief period and he was preparing to leave for Krajina, I shortly told him about some of my experience from the combat operations and my stay in that area, and then I took up the regular duties of a commander, which means I talked to the officers from the staff, the operatives, first and foremost, in order to become informed with the situation in the brigade. And looking at this work book for that day, as it says, the battalion commanders and artillery battalion commanders had reporting sessions, and it says the same for the 27th. Now, I'm not quite sure why two days in a row I organised reporting sessions because one would have been enough, but possibly one had been planned for the 26th and then postponed until the 27th or both of them, but I did lead one of those reporting sessions, at least one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall now whether there was one on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that here so I can't deny that it wasn't but it also says the 27th, so I am sure that I did lead one of those reporting sessions, maybe both, if both were held. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well let's just illustrate the point you're making. If we have a look at 7D680 the regular combat report for the 26th of September. We can see the penultimate bullet point of paragraph two reads: "The brigade commander held a briefing for battalion/artillery battalion commanders, and a command reconnaissance mission is currently underway led by the brigade commander." Does that ring any bells, the command reconnaissance mission?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows that the briefing was held and reconnaissance was conducted with the head of the brigade commander which must have been me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go to 7D681, please, the regular combat report for the following day, the 27th of September. We see it says under paragraph 2 there: "A routine briefing with battalion/artillery battalion commanders was held." Does it help you at all as to whether there were two meetings or just one?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says in this report that on this day, the 27th, a briefing was held, then it was. And at the time, I was the brigade commander so I was present there. But I'm not quite clear and can't provide an answer as to why two briefings were held on two consecutive days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Just a look at two more documents to try and help piece together your movements on these couple of days. Can we have a look at 7D770. This is the vehicle work log for the vehicle we're very familiar with, the Nissan Patrol T-2175 for the month of September. And we'll need to look at the third page, please. No apparent use of that vehicle between the 17th and the 29th of September. On the 17th, it appears to have gone from Zvornik to Belgrade. And then on the 29th, came back from somewhere to Zvornik. Where did it come back from on the 29th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in that second column, the 29th, in the original, it says Barajevo which was a service for those Nissan vehicles near Belgrade called Barajevo, a repairs shop. And after the vehicles were used for a long time, especially in Krajina in poor conditions, the vehicles need to be serviced. So that's where they were sent during the time that I was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you use any other vehicle in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another vehicle which I found in the brigade on my return from the Krajina, it was a Renault Safran which had remained behind. It had been left there by the army of Srpska Krajina. For some reason it was unable to cross the bridge into Serbia so it was there. I used that vehicle for a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look please at 7D771.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is a vehicle work log from the 1st of September to the 30th of September for a Renault Safran. The users are various: General Stupar, Lieutenant-Colonel Milovanovic, Major Obrenovic, Ljubisa Danojlovic, but the driver is listed as Sergeant Bogdan Pandurevic. Is this the vehicle you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. That's the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And again if we can go to the third page of that document, the second in B/C/S. And we can see that on the 25th of September, that vehicle appears to have gone from Zvornik to Belgrade, according to the vehicle work log, and on the 27th of September, it went on a journey Loko to Zvornik, Zvornik-Loko, does that help you as to whether you travelled anywhere on the 26th or 27th of September?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th, I didn't travel anywhere. On the 27th, this vehicle was used in the Zvornik area in the Loko area, also on the 28th and the 29th. Could this be moved to the right please so I can see the driver's signatures. Yes, it's last three something signatures, B Pandurevic, that's Bogdan Pandurevic, he was my driver alongside Dragan Stevic, and he drove me on the 27th, the 28th, and 29th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you identify the suggest for the 25th of September?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you were in Budva, what means of transport did you use to get there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used my private car.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so far as you were aware, where was the Renault Safran during the time that you were in Budva?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that but we can reconstruct it from this vehicle work sheet, but I did not make any decisions on the use of that vehicle at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Now, upon your return to the brigade, did you come to learn about something unusual going on in Zvornik during your absence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A few days later, I learned that some trucks had passed through Zvornik and that these trucks were carrying some sort of material which left behind an unbearable stench. I discussed this with Mijo Dragutinovic. He said that probably corpses had been transported, and he knew that the trucks came from the transport company because they had Styer [phoen] make trucks and that the local citizens were upset by that and that this happened in the course of the night. I asked him whether the brigade had been assigned any sort of task or issued any sort of order in connection with this and his answer was no. He said he had no knowledge and he knew no details about that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you make any further inquiries into what had been going on and did you come to learn who was involved?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't discuss this in detail with anyone at that time, nor did I make any sort of investigation. When Dragan Obrenovic returned from the Krajina, I asked him whether he had been informed of all this, and he told me that just before my return from the Krajina, he had been at the command in Vlasenica and that he was aware that Mladic personally had approved fuel for the relocation of corpses and that the engineers battalion of the Drina Corps participated in that. He also said that this operation was being conducted by the very top, the highest authorities in the army and that no task had been issued to the corps in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you say no task had been issued to the corps in your last answer?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you consider whether you should conduct a criminal investigation into what had been going on?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult for me to take any action in view of the information I had. Somebody was doing a job that had nothing to do with me, and in view of what had happened in July, I assumed that this operation had to be much more secretive and that it was better for me not to get mixed up in it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was your information as to how secretive the operation had been in September?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Mijo Dragutinovic told me it lasted for five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you able to discern from what he or Obrenovic told you what agencies had been involved in the operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that it did not go down the usual chain of command, according to the normal method of issuing tasks to subordinate units, it could have been organised within the scope of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you know that or just assume that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any direct information about who was engaged in this, who was in charge of it, but I was able to conclude that it was being done by the security organs because no tasks had been issued to any of the commands for them to pass the orders down the chain of command and deal with this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long was Dragan Obrenovic in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for about a month, I'm not sure exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when he mentioned the fuel that you've told us about, did he draw your attention to any particular document or record or did he just tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the source of his information was concerning the fuel, whether it was General Krstic who had told him or whether he had learned it in some other way. All he told me was that fuel had been approved for that operation and that it would be used for the purposes of relocating corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did he know where the fuel had come from?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he knew. We assumed it might have come from a base which had fuel available and which was supplying units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after the end of September, how did the combat situation develop in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any direct information about the course of the combat activities in the Krajina, but I did know in general terms that there was heavy fighting going on, that the town of Banja Luka was under threat, that the Army of Republika Srpska invested great efforts engaging all its resources and managed to stop the offensive carried out jointly by the Croatian Army, the Croatian Defence Council, and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How did the combat situation come to an end?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it came to an end with the signing of a cease-fire which was subsequently followed by the negotiations in Dayton with a view to putting an end to the war finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall what date, approximately, the Dayton Peace Agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is initialled sometime in November 1995 and later on it was signed in Paris, whether in January 1996, I'm not sure. I did have that document in my hands, the framework agreement for peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina with some 11 annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did your job involve after November 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the framework agreement for peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what I as a soldier found most significant were the military annexes of the agreement, these referred to the deployment of IFOR forces, these were forces for the implementation of peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to my tasks as a brigade commander with respect to the separation of forces, the shift in the front line, and compliance with all the provisions of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did you have to do in relation to your own forces following the initialling of the agreement in November 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were deadlines set for particular activities to be carried out in several stages. The first stage was moving the existing positions from the confrontation line two or four kilometres back and this applied to both warring sides. That was the first activity we carried out and it was preceded by a joint meeting between the commander of the American forces in that sector, Lieutenant-Colonel Hareman [phoen], Semso Muminovic and myself. The meeting was held in Memici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when was the state of war lifted?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the separation of the sides, within 45 days or 120 days, I'm not sure, there had to be complete withdrawal of all forces to barracks, the grouping of equipment in certain locations, and I think the state of war was ended in December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did the implementation of the military accords under the Dayton Peace Agreement take?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took quite a long time. I think the deadline was 120 days for both men and equipment to be withdrawn to barracks. Collection points for equipment were designated and then mixed controls were carried out so that the equipment was inspected by teams from the Army of Republika Srpska in the Bosnia-Herzegovina forces and vice versa. And within the scope of implementation of this agreement, there was a process of subregional monitoring of weapons on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, where it was stated precisely what equipment what side was able to have at its disposal. I attended such negotiations in Vienna on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you conclude the putting into effect of all those measures as commander of the Zvornik Brigade or did you leave before the tasks were all finished?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The complete withdrawal of all units and equipment to barracks and demobilization of the majority of the soldiers, apart from those who wished to remain in professional service, was completed while I was still the brigade commander. All that was left was to carry out inspection on both sides to check whether the provisions of the military annex of the Dayton Accord had been complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you leave Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the Zvornik Brigade in April 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was then assigned to the Main Staff to the Administration for Operations and Training, the operations department, as a deputy chief of the operations department in the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, we know that since the war, you have remarried and had two sons. When did you first meet your second wife?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- well, I first met her in April 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we might as well get this out of the way. What happened to your first marriage?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first marriage took place in November 1985, and we agreed on a divorce in October 1994, as far as I can remember. It was a consensual divorce.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you still have contact with your daughter Natasha?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I have been in contact with her all the time. It was a consensual divorce, both sides agreed. There was only one hearing which lasted for half an hour, and the decision came into force, neither of us appealed, we waived the appeal. We had a drink together and we separated in a civilised manner, and I remained in contact with my daughter. I visited her regularly during the war and after the war and now she's visiting me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in June of 1996, what happened in terms of your career?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was assigned to the Main Staff to the operations department, there were three other officers, colonels, together with me who came to the Main Staff. They had all been brigade commanders or regiment commanders. I think it was Colonel Blagojevic, Colonel Glizdek [phoen] and Colonel Borovina. They were all assigned to appropriate duties which were one step higher than the positions they had had as brigade commanders, that was group 8 whereas brigade commander is 9. I was assigned to a lower level duty and that's group 10. I spent a month there and then I asked General Mladic for approval to take study leave. He did not approve this. Then I applied to General Milovanovic. He gave his permission, and a month later I left Crna Rijeka and spent most of my time in Belgrade working on my Ph.D.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until November 1996. From time to time I went to Zvornik but I spent most of the time in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in 1996, keeping as it were the chronology, were there any political changes in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, in September, elections were held for the president of the republic, and Mrs. Biljana Plavsic was elected president. Later -- previously, certain pressures had been exerted by the international community and President Karadzic, who had been president up to that time, withdrew from political life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you have any connections to any political party at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of any political party, nor did I have any political connections with anyone. I was not involved in politics at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What happened in terms of the structure of the Army of Republika Srpska after the election of the new president?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the new president was elected, after the war, the army had to carry out certain establishment changes and reorganise. It had to reduce its numbers, a new establishment had to be drawn up for a peacetime army, and also a wartime army had to be planned. It was necessary for the Main Staff to be renamed and to become the General Staff as is usual, and for that purpose, the president of the republic asked for a session of the Supreme Command and for the Main Staff to be renamed as the General Staff. This implied certain personnel changes because there were already indications at that time that there would be indictments raised both against General Mladic and others and that he would not be able to remain at that post. That was the information I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early November, my brother Nenad called me up on the telephone and told me that Vasic had been looking for me for two days. Vasic was the chief of the public security centre in Zvornik and he had a message to give me. My brother told me to contact Vasic, which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what chain of events did that set?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vasic told me that the president of the republic was looking for me, that I should report to Pale, that a meeting had been planned and that a number of officers from the Army of Republika Srpska had been summoned to that meeting. I wasn't told about the details or the purpose of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, just to be clear, are we talking November 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you go?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was the meeting like?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we waited a long time. When I went up there I met Mr. Pero Colic who was a colonel whom I saw once before the war. I knew nothing about him. And then Colonel Josipovic, Dragan Josipovic who was the commander of the Ilijas Brigade near Sarajevo, I knew him from before. Then there was a man from the state security who used to be my history teacher in secondary school, his name was Mile Renovica, and we were waiting for General Grubac to arrive and also, I think, General Talic and some other colonels. And we were supposed to have a meeting with all those senior officers because the president had planned certain personnel changes within the General Staff. And before that, a meeting of the Supreme Command had been scheduled to which nobody appeared from the then Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What happened at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we sat in a large hall until well after midnight in the offices of the president, madam president. There were the top leaders from the republic. And somewhere after midnight, I think it was, they called Pero Colic and Josipovic into the cabinet or office of the president where they stayed for some time, and then they all adjourned to the big hall and the president, Biljana Plavsic, read out the decisions or presented the decisions which they had made at that joint meeting of theirs which I did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How did it affect you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam President said she had decide that Pero Colic should be promoted to the rank of General and that he be appointed as chief of the General Staff, having renamed the Main Staff the General Staff, and also Josipovic, he was promoted to the rank of General by her, and he was the deputy chief, deputy head. And I was told that I had been appointed as assistant to the chief for morale and moral guidance and religious affairs, and the president asked for our reactions, to hear our reactions. I was the only one to take the floor, and I said that I considered that in the Army of Republika Srpska there were a lot of highly-qualified and experienced officers and that there was no need to rush a decision of any kind and that the post I was given, I wasn't very happy to have it, but I would carry out any assignment and occupy any post that they put me in. And her answer was: You can do that, you know how to do that, and you will do that. The decision was upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I sense Mr. McCloskey's unease. It's the translation of the office to which you were appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us what it is slowly to give the interpreters a chance?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became Gvero in translation, the assistant for morale and religious and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about your rank, was that changed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I still remained a colonel by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You may have already substantially dealt with this, but did you understand why the new president felt it necessary to substantially change the personnel within the command of the Main Staff or the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was common knowledge in Republika Srpska that almost throughout the war, there was a certain amount -- a certain lack of understanding, if I can put it that way, not to use a stronger word, between the commander of the Main Staff and the president of the republic which resulted in certain problems in control and command of the army. And there were attempts by the president to replace the commander of the Main Staff and that nobody wanted to take on that duty, I don't know for what reason that was. And after the war, it was imminent, reorganisation was imminent, and since General Mladic did not respond and did not come to attend the meeting of the Supreme Command, and his presence had been required and probably the presence of some other generals in order to resolve this issue, but as he failed to appear, the president decided to make the decisions without him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you understand why you were selected for the post you were given?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were four of us in all and they took it in order, some kind of order, and I was probably the only one and that's why I was put in the post. Perhaps if there was somebody after me, he would have been assigned the next post down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you regard it as a promotion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense of rank and function and post, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was the reaction to these changes?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were troubled times in a difficult situation. And the command of the Main Staff up until then, General Mladic was in Crna Rijeka, and he didn't want to have any contacts with the president. He refused the hand over and takeover of duty, the four of us for a time were at Pale and we had communication with certain corps and certain corps would send reports to us. Others would send it to the Main Staff and others yet again would send it to both, and there were different comments in the media about all this. There were articles that appeared that were very personal in nature and spoke about the four of us who had been posted to that General Staff. So I find it unpleasant to think back to those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How were you characterised in the press?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well there were some articles that appeared, I remember my daughter called me up from Belgrade and asked me what was going on and what the whole thing was about. They weren't articles that were rude or offensive, but they did overstep some military norms and codes of conduct or they stressed too much ambition, but there weren't any assessments made against my character or anything like that or my professional qualities whereas the others were criticised, the other people were criticised, and said they didn't know their job, they were incompetent, not professional and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where was the new staff situated?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they managed to organise a meeting at Pale, attended by General Milovanovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Miletic"] and I and General Tolimir, I remember that very well. Now, whether there was anybody else, I'm not quite sure, anyway it was agreed that instead of Mladic, the handover and takeover of duty between Pero Colic should be conducted by General Milovanovic. And a plan was drawn up for touring the units and the handover of duty, and the General Staff moved to Bijeljina. And after that, the other officers who were in Crna Rijeka, except for the Generals as far as I remember, or the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, one moment. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just that in transcript, on page 23, line 5, the name of my client is mentioned, and I'm sure the witness did not mention my client's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, I agree with that. He said General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirm that, Mr. Pandurevic. For the record, I saw Mr. Pandurevic nodding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you remain as assistant commander for moral and legal affairs or did you acquire some other rank, some other position?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, soon after those appointments, the 5th Corps was set up with its headquarters in Sokolac, and General Josipovic wanted to be given the post. He didn't like being the deputy head, and then a proposal went to the president that he be appointed the command of the 5th Corps and that I be appointed deputy chief of the General Staff. And that is what was done I think sometime in November 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On the 2nd of August of 1997, did you get married to your present wife Danijela?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you remain at the command of the General Staff in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until September. In September, I went to Belgrade to the National Defence School.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that we're clear, is that September of 1997?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why did you go to the National Defence School in September of 1997?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the time when the academic year started, or academic years in general, and the same holds true for military academies and military schools. So sometime in June 1997, we sent in a proposal with a list of officers from the Army of Republika Srpska who wished to attend training in Belgrade in the command staff academy. I think there were 30 names on that list, 30 officers, and there were six who wanted to go to the National Defence School and among them, I, myself. However, we received confirmation that everything was all right, but one or two days before the beginning of the academic year, a document arrived from Belgrade which was not signed and which stated that as for the command staff school, only 13 people could enroll there and one person could enroll in the National Defence School and my name was not on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know whose name was on that list?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that list was Novak Djukic from the 1st Krajina Corps, he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who made the selection as to who would go?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name of the person who did that, but I'm quite sure that somebody -- that it was a high-ranking officer from the Main Staff of the war composition of the Main Staff, but this was covered by a decision of the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did you do about that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the initiative of the chief of the General Staff, General Colic, a meeting was called for at General Persic's and then there was a meeting at President Milosevic's office. And present there were the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, the prime minister, the minister of defence, I think General Savcic was there, too, of course Pero Colic and myself, and there was the chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, General Perisic. And at that meeting, because allegedly General Perisic couldn't make the decision himself, it was decided that everybody should go to enroll into the school according to the previous list that had been okayed, so I was sent to school with the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long were you at the National School of Defence and with what honours did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The school, according to its curriculum, lasts for one year and it finishes when you take your exams, graduation exam at the end and that exam you have to sit for in July. I passed all the exams and I just had my graduation, final exam to take. And that morning when I was ready to defend my graduate thesis, the head of the School for National Defence, General Jagos Stevanovic, told me that his deputy would tell me -- would read out a decision to me, and the decision was that my graduation session be postponed for a fortnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was that all about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allegedly because of a military disciplinary measures taken against me because of alleged abuse with respect to having been allotted a flat. I know that before that event, maybe a month before the event, there was a team from the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia with three colonels, one of them from the security administration, one from the legal administration, and the third, I don't know who that was, or what he was. They talked to me in the presence of the headmaster or head of the school with respect to the request that I had tabled to be allotted in conformity with the law, a larger flat because my wife was pregnant at the time and she was to give birth in two or three months' time, so I had put in a request for a bigger flat, bigger accommodation. And that's what I was supposed to get. They asked me to sign a statement of some kind and said everything would be all right. I refused to do that and they left. And after that, I was prevented from taking my final examination and defending my thesis and military disciplinary measures were put in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What came of them?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went on for some time because there's set procedure. First of all -- well, I'm not a lawyer but as far as I understand it, it is first of all discussed and dealt with within the -- by officers, and then the military disciplinary Prosecutor files a proposal and a date is set for a hearing, and when the hearing was supposed to talk place, the prosecutor who had raised the whole -- put the whole procedure in place didn't appear, another prosecutor appeared and he said he withdrew the proceedings. So everything stopped without any trial. And six months after the first period that I was supposed to take my graduation exam, I took it in January 1999, and I graduated with honours and a small celebration was organised to present me with a diploma and a military sabre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You mentioned that at the time you were about to graduate, your wife was pregnant. Were your twin boys born on the 27th of July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We've been through your various promotions, but did you retire from the Army of Yugoslavia in 2002?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The rank in the Army of Yugoslavia was recognised later on at -- well, later than it was recognised for other people. On the basis of a decree of the president of the republic, Mr. Kostunica, so I had the rank of colonel in the army of Yugoslavia for six years, and I had fulfilled all the legal conditions for the rank to be verified in the army of Yugoslavia and this was done in 2001. And I was sent to retirement as an invalid in 2002. I had an invalidity pension.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Twenty-five minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When, in the course of the history that you have been relating to us this morning, did you first learn that there was an indictment before this Tribunal with your name on it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When indictments began to be raised against various individuals, there was various speculation going on and rumours going around as to who the accused could be and whose names in those indictments, and there were suspicions of secret indictments being in existence, but I learned publicly that I was indicted in December 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you feel when you found that out?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I felt terrible, very unpleasant feeling because it was a turning point in my life in actual fact, it was something that completely derailed me and defined my life's course from that day to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where were you and what were your circumstances in December 2001?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December 2001, I was the chief of the centre for military strategic studies and research, and I was living a normal life, functioning normally, moving around normally in public places, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was your family situation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived with my wife and two sons. They were three years old at the time. They were too small to be able to understand anything or me to be able to explain my situation to them in any way, and I thought that the important thing was that for at least one or two years, I spend time with them, as much as possible, and then to try when they were a bit older to explain to them what it was all about, but I never had any illusions, I thought that -- I never thought that I would appear in court and have to defend myself against accusations made against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if you would just repeat what you said in the last sentence there because there seems to be widespread concern that you said precisely the opposite of what's been translated. Did you think you would have to appear in court?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter wasn't sure what the accused actually meant so could he repeat it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly I thought -- I knew that I had to appear in court, I had no illusions on that score, but I considered that I would need some time before I did that because of my two sons. Otherwise, had I remained unmarried, as soon as I'd heard about the indictment, I wouldn't have waited a moment, I would have come straight into court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How did you live after the discovery that you had been indicted?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I withdrew and reduced my contacts with people, I didn't appear in public places. I was mostly with my family and lived that kind of secluded life.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did you remain with your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps half a year from when the indictment was made public. We were together all the time, and then I lived in a rented flat close to my own flat and perhaps every 20 days or a month, they would visit me and they would spend time with me for about through or four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How did you deal with the question with the boys?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as soon as they were able to understand things, and children are more mature today, they have video games and various other devices and know more, I tried to explain the whole situation to them. Whether they fully understood or not, I'm not quite sure, but I think they understand it all today. Although it was a very difficult time for them, every time we met and had to part was very difficult and involved a great deal of emotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was the decisive point for you in terms of your surrender?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, the time that I spent with my family since the indictment was raised and published until I came to The Hague Tribunal was in my opinion enough time -- I gave enough time for the family to be able to understand and for them to be able to live without me, and so then I decided to come here and to take up these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, let's step back, as it were, within that period. By 2002, the Krstic trial had been completed. Did you gather a lot of information about that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the media, well, television, did not cover General Krstic's trial enough. There were just periodical reports and I read parts of his interview in the papers, his interview given to the OTP. I followed the trial of President Milosevic because there were certain matters raised there that had to do with Srebrenica, and then from time to time I would follow reports from the Blagojevic and Jokic trial, and I also think I followed the Obrenovic testimony before judgement. I saw some footage played here during the trials and that was the first time that I saw those images, people Potocari, and some other pictures and images that were shown here. In the meantime, I came by Mr. Richard Butler's report too so I had quite a clear picture of all the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll just pick up on a few things you said there. The Krstic trial, were you able to follow that on television?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't broadcast like Milosevic's trial was broadcast. There may have been some reports and something in the written media but you couldn't get a clear picture of the course of the trial, at least I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where did you get a copy of the military analyst Richard Butler's report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Milomir Savcic who gave me that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you remember when he gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the middle of 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when you had read it, what did you think of it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was amazed when I saw the facts and information contained in that report. What I know about all these events amounted to about 10 percent of what was in the report. Before reading that report, I had no knowledge or clear idea about the events surrounding the evacuation from Potocari, the transport of the captured prisoners, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, at about the time that you first saw Richard Butler's report, were you in contact with General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was occasionally in contact with General Zivanovic. He is a beekeeper, and he was constantly building bee hives and looking for wooden boards. I had a relative who was a former signalsman from the Drina Corps who had a timber factory, so he kept asking me to get material for him from my relative. That's why we were in contact. And when we did have contact, we also talked about certain wartime events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you become aware that he had certain connections?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that he had contacts with The Hague Tribunal because he told me that himself. I knew that he possessed certain documents which he had taken with him from the corps command, and I think he later put those documents at the disposal of the OTP. I also knew that the OTP had conducted several interviews with him. I knew that various journalists came to see him. I also went to see him on several occasions in his home in Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you tell him about your reaction to the report of Richard Butler?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we discussed that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so that we can place this absolutely into context, at the time that you read Richard Butler's report and the time that you then subsequently discussed it with General Zivanovic, were you aware of the existence of any indictment against you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that at the time. I suspected it but I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did General Zivanovic make any suggestion to you as a result of your discussion about your reaction to Richard Butler's report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reactions in connection to that report had mostly to do with the documents mentioned in the report which had been drawn up by me. I felt that the documents had been misinterpreted as had the reports. I also felt that certain standpoints as regards the doctrine of the JNA and VRS had been misinterpreted. I could not go into the facts because I was not familiar with them. That was what Zivanovic and I discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did he suggest you should do about it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic is a rather unusual collocutor, I think Mr. McCloskey will agree with that also. He had certain suggestions to make. He said you should be as close to them as possible, as close to the source -- as close to the source of information, as close to the threat you are faced with, in order to defend yourself from it more successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who did he have in mind?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably thought it was time to establish -- it was better to establish contact with the people from the OTP in a timely manner than let matters run their course. Whether he was sincere in all of that, I can't say. It's not for me to judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did he have any means at his disposal to effect that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he said that he was able to establish contact at any time, that he had the telephone numbers of people from The Hague Tribunal, and when it came to him, himself, and the indictment for Srebrenica as well as the investigations of crimes committed by Muslims against the Serbs in Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did he do that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: About how long after you'd discussed Richard Butler's report with him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was a meeting and probably that meeting would have been held had there not been Mr. Richard Butler's report and that was in October 2001. It was a meeting with persons whom I didn't know at the time, I didn't know their names or what they were doing, and they were in contact with Mr. Zivanovic. This was Ms. Gilleece and her team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who did you take to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first met Mr. Zivanovic at his home and Mr. Djordje Sarapa accompanied me, my brother Petar also came along. He was not directly involved in any talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long had you known Mr. Sarapa by October of 2001?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I had known him for at least three years before that. That was the period when the military disciplinary proceedings were instituted against me and when I was involved in the case concerning my flat before the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did he have to do with that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the meeting with Zivanovic or the previous one I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The proceedings concerning the military discipline?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I always respect one's profession. I had the right to a lawyer in that sort of disciplinary proceeding. I didn't want to take a military counsel, but at the recommendation of a friend of mine, I contacted Mr. Sarapa and engaged him. I was told he had come from Croatia, and to avoid offending anyone, I didn't want to have contacts with lawyers who said they had connections in the court. I wanted to deal with someone I didn't know actually personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why did you take him to the meeting with Ms. Gilleece?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason why he accompanied me to that meeting was for us to meet Zivanovic and for Zivanovic to tell us about the nature of his contacts with The Hague Tribunal and the OTP and for Djordje, as a lawyer, to evaluate the legal aspects of those contacts and the manner in which they can be carried out, and then he remained at the meeting with Ms. Gilleece.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What sort of establishment did you meet Ms. Gilleece in?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my meeting with Mr. Zivanovic, he told me to what building we should go or, rather, he drove his car in front of our car and we arrived in front of a restaurant called, I think, Peti Puk, and he said he had agreed a meeting with Ms. Gilleece somewhere else and that he would go and fetch her and bring her there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What time did you get there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think we arrived at the restaurant at about 11.00, I'm not quite sure, but it was certainly before noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long after you got there did Ms. Gilleece arrive?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not long afterwards, some 15 or 20 minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And who was with her?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, three persons, Ms. Gilleece, a certain Major of the Canadian army whose name I don't know, and a female interpreter from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you know her name?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She introduced herself. I think her name was Vesna.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so we, as it were, place as her into context, you speak reasonably good English now, General Pandurevic. Did you speak English in 2001?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had been trying to learn English for a long time, although we had to take Russian in secondary school, but from the time I went to Slovenia I took courses in the English language; however, I forgot a lot during the war. I did, however, understand that the interpreter Vesna did not have a good command of military terminology. This is a very specialised area, and you will agree with me that it's very difficult for someone without a military background to translate those terms into another language.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did you do when Ms. Gilleece and her entourage arrived at the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had already been sitting and a table and we had ordered drinks, of course we rose to greet the new-comers, we were all introduced and then we all sat down at a table together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did what?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As usual, General Zivanovic started his theatrics with extensive introductions and explanations which I found it hard to understand, and I believe Ms. Gilleece didn't understand at all, and then we arrived at the main topic which was for us to provide the information we had concerning the crimes against the Serbs in the Podrinje, Ms. Gilleece was interested in this information, and also for me to put forward some of my observations regarding the events in Srebrenica because that was Mr. Zivanovic's initiative. He felt that all teams, regardless of what investigations they were engaged in, were in mutual contact and exchanged information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you have lunch?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we started by having drinks and then the owner of the cafe prepared lunch. The lunch went on for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sat there having lunch and talking for some time, then we would get up and take a walk around the building looking at some old ethnic exhibits, things that the owner had there, an old oven and such like, and we stayed in that area until 1800 hours when a wedding procession turned up with wedding guests and the bride, and then we moved to another area, a private space belonging to the owner of the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was when we continued our previous activities, and we stayed there until 2100 or 2200 hours, I'm not sure exactly, but it was already night, night-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So the note we've got which we're going to look at in some detail in a little minute reflects events over 10 hours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes, maybe an hour less than that but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And throughout that time, were you all drinking alcohol?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all drank. I don't know whether my brother Petar did because he wasn't sitting at the table together with us, but we all drank including me because I felt it would be inappropriate, although I'm not a man who likes a lot of alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about Ms. Gilleece?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She drank too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And Vesna, the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so did she.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of anybody taking any notes of what was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. At one point, Ms. Gilleece took out a note pad, A4 size, and occasionally she took notes of what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea of this 10-hour discourse, I mean, how did it progress?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning after the introductions and some introductory remarks by Mr. Zivanovic, and after some chatting about ordinary things, for about an hour and a half, perhaps, I tried to explain in broad strokes what I knew about the period in July 1995, and after that we moved on to providing the information that Ms. Gilleece was interested in concerning the crimes against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did this take the form of, as it were, an interview or a conversation or a roundtable discussion or what?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult to control the course of the conversation, especially because of the presence of Mr. Zivanovic, and I also think that the interpretation was not adequate and this led to a lot of interruptions and confusion. At one point, I thought it would have been better if I hadn't come at all because I don't like things that don't proceed in a proper manner following the usual procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When it was all over, were you offered the opportunity to read Ms. Gilleece' note or have it translated to you or offered the chance of having a copy sent to you for your approval?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. I don't remember when that note pad disappeared from view and at that point, I didn't think that would be a note that would be forwarded to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When was the first time you knew that something had been typed up of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that here. I saw it in the material that had been disclosed in connection with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Now let's proceed to look at the note. We have up until now used a redacted copy, and if there's going to be any legal argument about this, it might be appropriate that it's dealt with now because I propose to take General Pandurevic through the unredacted copy which is in e-court as 7D1154. I'll wait to hear if anybody's got anything to say about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Prosecution agrees with that approach and if the Court wants to know anything about why it was originally redacted, we, of course, I think all sides know why that was, but I think now that the General is on the witness stand it would be best to have the full document if he's going to be questioned upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well I anticipated that response. I was actually waiting for objection from behind me which I can't see but I hear none so I will proceed. Can we please put 7D1154 into e-court. I'm going to provide the General with a hard copy to which I've appended paragraph numbers to make it easier. I'm happy for Mr. McCloskey to just inspect that to make sure I haven't put anything untoward on it but that's all that is on there. I'm sorry, yes, of course. I've apparently described P2408 as the unredacted copy. That, of course, is the redacted copy, and 7D1154 is the unredacted copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, Mr. McCloskey, it has been the practice here not to broadcast texts which indicate names of our staff -- or of the Tribunal's staff and interpreters and whatever. We can proceed but I don't know what your position on this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I had just noticed that we had completely unredacted it and that name should have remained redacted. It only appears on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So if we don't broadcast the first page, thereafter there is no difficulty as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Okay with you, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And there's only one name that I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but I spoke the way I spoke precisely to be very cautious and not to give any leads. So let's proceed with the -- we won't broadcast this first page and then we'll see later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Paragraphs 1 and 2 don't really concern the events that you have related to us, but we can see as we get on to paragraph 3 the details of the meeting with you. Did you recall it was on the 2nd of October, 2001?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't know if it was the 2nd of October, I knew that it was roughly the beginning of October but if it says the 2nd then it was the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if we go to paragraph 4, that seems to accord with your recollection that General Zivanovic went to meet Ms. Gilleece and her colleagues somewhere else and then brought them to a restaurant called Peti Puk where you were already seated with Mr. Sarapa. Let's start by looking at paragraph 5. "General Zivanovic explained that he taught Mr. Pandurevic at the military academy many years ago." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Zivanovic never taught me. He's an artillery man and I'm an infantry man. Now, whether he said that to sort of boast a bit, I don't know, but he certainly was no teacher of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "Pandurevic was also in charge of the Zvornik area when the Serbs recaptured Kamenica in 1993. General Zivanovic then advised that Mr. Pandurevic wanted to explains his actions in 1995 to us. General Zivanovic also mentioned that Dragan Obrenovic had been Mr. Pandurevic's Chief of Staff in 1995." Do you recall that being part of the introduction that General Zivanovic made?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he gave the reasons why I could provide information about the suffering of Serbs in Podrinje and the events of 1993, and in that context he said that I was in the area in 1993 and. I think that after that he went on to say that I wanted to interpret, or, rather, present certain information to Ms. Gilleece. Now, whether he mentioned Obrenovic as being Chief of Staff or not, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Paragraph 6: "Before Mr. Pandurevic spoke, I explained to the group that as team members of Team 9 we investigate allegations of war crimes committed by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Eastern Bosnia from 1992 to 1993. I further explained how the ICTY functions with various teams investigating alleged crimes committed by Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. I also explained the issues of witnesses and suspects in accordance with ICTY rules and procedures."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think just for the record, I think you left out that the crimes she was looking at were against the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sure it was by accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: According to your recollection of events, did Ms. Gilleece explain to you the rules for suspects and witnesses of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that she explained her position and her role and what she did and the type of work she did. Now, as I'm here in court for the first time and in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, I heard discussions with respect to the rights of suspects and the rights of witnesses and what the procedure was for investigators or the OTP in interviewing people. I'm quite certain that at that time, I had heard nothing about any of that, and I consider that this was just written in by inertia as a normal of run of things because it's probably the duty of every investigator to put something down like that. And I'm sure that Ms. Gilleece did not -- was not aware of my status at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to paragraph 10, please. "I then specifically explained to Mr. Pandurevic that in --" I'm sorry, "I then specifically explained to Mr. Pandurevic that he was under no obligation to speak to us about anything. If he did speak, it would be of his own free will. I advised him that he could have an attorney represent him. I advised him that whatever he told me, I was obliged to report to the ICTY, including Team 6, and anything he said could be used before the Tribunal. I advised him that he could stop speaking to us at any time. I further advised Mr. Pandurevic, General Zivanovic, and Mr. Sarapa that we understood that we were their guests and they could ask us to leave at any time. If they asked us to leave, I assured them that we would immediately comply with their request." Do you recall those words being said to you during the course of the introductions at this restaurant?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this was stated in this shape or form. What was said was that the lady wants to hear me out and that she could convey that to Team number 6, and I understood it that this was a team led by Mr. McCloskey. Now, as to me not having -- me having the right to say silent, I knew that it was my good will and not my duty or obligation to speak. And the fact that they were my guests, they were not my guests.
